tagline: The big cat that kills with a bite to the skull
summary: The largest cat in the Americas, a powerfully built hunter of rainforest, river and swamp. Rather than simply gripping the throat, a jaguar will often drive its canines straight through its prey's skull, and its jaws can crack turtle shells and pierce the armoured hide of a caiman.

stats.size: Head and body 1.5–1.8 m plus a 70–90 cm tail; usually 68–136 kg
stats.habitat: Dense lowland rainforest, flooded forest, swamps and wetlands, nearly always close to water
stats.elevation: Mostly below 2,000 m; recorded up to 3,800 m in Costa Rica
stats.range: Mexico to northern Argentina, across 18 countries; rare wanderers reach Arizona and New Mexico
stats.diet: Over 85 prey species, from peccaries, capybaras and deer to caimans, turtles and fish
stats.conservation: IUCN Red List: Near Threatened (2017 assessment)

facts.title: Straight through the skull
facts.text: A jaguar may kill with a suffocating neck bite, but it often drives its canines through the back of its prey's skull instead. The same jaws can bite through thick reptile skin and turtle shells.

facts.title: Pound for pound, the strongest jaws
facts.text: A 2012 study of the jaw muscles of nine cat species found that the jaguar — the most bone- and shell-crunching cat in the sample — had relatively greater bite-force capacity than the others. A tiger bites harder in absolute terms, but for its size the jaguar comes out ahead.

facts.title: A cat that loves water
facts.text: Jaguars are excellent swimmers. In the flooded forests of the Amazon they swim from tree to tree to hunt monkeys and sloths, and they regularly catch caimans, turtles and anacondas.

facts.title: A menu of 85 species
facts.text: More than 85 kinds of prey have been recorded in the jaguar's diet. One jaguar was seen dragging a 34 kg sea turtle 91.5 m into the cover of the forest.

facts.title: Black jaguars are not a separate species
facts.text: All-black jaguars are fairly common, especially in forest. Their colour comes from a single dominant gene, and the rosettes are usually still faintly visible against the dark coat.

facts.title: Half its kingdom lost
facts.text: Jaguars have been wiped out from nearly half of their historic range, mainly through habitat loss, conflict with ranchers and the hunting of their prey.

notes: All three photographs are wild jaguars from the Brazilian Pantanal (no licensed in-situ Amazon photo of comparable quality was found); the record is still filed under 'amazon' first as briefed. Commons labels the alt-2 animal with the subspecies name P. o. palustris, but jaguar subspecies are not generally recognised, so species is given as Panthera onca. The bite-force fact rests on Hartstone-Rose et al. 2012, whose abstract says the jaguar 'appears to have relatively higher force production capabilities' among nine felids; the tiger comparison is from the lead author's comments reported by BBC Wildlife (discoverwildlife.com), not cited here. Size: ADW notes Pantanal males average 100 kg while Honduran males average 57 kg, so the 68–136 kg range is typical rather than absolute. Elevation minimum (10 m) follows ADW. The IUCN DOI and GBIF links resolve in a browser but return 403 to scripted requests (bot protection); IDs were checked through the GBIF API and Wikidata. IUCN year is the publication year of the assessment (2017).
